sec.title: Background
sec.p: Worsening heart failure (WHF) challenges health care with frequent rehospitalizations and reduced quality of life for patients. Despite therapeutic advances, high rehospitalization risks highlight the urgent need for new treatments.

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: This study evaluated the effectiveness of initiating novel therapies during hospitalization or vulnerable phase for WHF patients to reduce rehospitalization risks and determine the optimal treatment sequence.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systematic review and network meta-analysis were performed in accordance with Cochrane Collaboration and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis guidelines. We included randomized clinical trials from January 2013, to December 2022, sourced from PUBMED and EMBASE, comparing novel heart failure therapies against control. The primary outcome was heart failure rehospitalization.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Analysis of 9 randomized clinical trials involving 18,540 patients showed significant rehospitalization reductions with novel treatments, especially sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors, angiotensin-neprilysin receptor inhibitor (ARNI), and ferric carboxymaltose. Sotagliflozin led to more pronounced reductions in heart failure hospitalization (OR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.39-0.63; P < 0.0001), followed by ARNI (OR: 0.54; 95% CI: 0.35-0.83; P = 0.005), ferric carboxymaltose (OR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.44-0.70; P < 0.0001), empagliflozin (OR: 0.56; 95% CI: 0.39-0.78; P = 0.0007), vericiguat 10 mg (OR: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.74-0.92; P = 0.0008), and finerenone 15 mg (OR: 0.59; 95% CI: 0.38-0.91; P = 0.016). These therapies, when initiated during hospitalization, markedly influenced rehospitalization outcomes.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Early administration of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors, ARNI, and ferric carboxymaltose for WHF patients significantly reduces rehospitalization risk. Our findings support a strategic shift in WHF management, advocating for the rapid introduction of these novel therapies to enhance patient prognosis.

def.p: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

body.p: Heart failure (HF) remains a major cause of mortality and hospitalization globally despite advances in pharmacological treatment.1 Worsening HF (WHF) is defined as a life-threatening condition characterized by deterioration of signs and symptoms in a patient with chronic HF, despite stable background therapy, requiring urgent escalation of therapy, typically with diuretics.2 Quadruple therapy, comprising angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), or angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, has been proposed for eligible, stable patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have demonstrated the efficacy of this therapy in reducing cardiovascular mortality and hospitalization for heart failure in ambulatory patients.3 However, the residual risk of hospital readmission remains elevated despite standard guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF. In addition, there is a lack of evidence regarding the best sequence for optimizing GDMT during a HF admission or the vulnerable phase (first 6 months postdischarge). In the WHF scenario, trials like PIONEER (Comparison of Sacubitril/Valsartan Versus Enalapril on Effect on NT-pro BNP in Patients Stabilized From an Acute Heart Failure Episode), which examined sacubitril-valsartan, used a surrogate primary endpoint. Meanwhile, the SOLOIST trial (Sotagliflozin in Patients with Diabetes and Recent Worsening Heart Failure) with sotagliflozin was prematurely terminated. This results in weak/moderate evidence supporting these medications in this context.4,5 Also, novel therapies like omecamtiv-mecarbil (in GALACTIC trial),6 finerenone (in FIGARO-CKD trial),7 and vericiguat (in VICTORIA trial)8 have been tested for reducing hospitalization for HF in patients with high residual cardiovascular risk. Finally, no studies have compared head-to-head the efficacy of the current HFrEF medical therapy in this scenario. This network meta-analysis and systematic review compared the effects of novel therapies initiated during hospitalization or vulnerable phase in patients with WHF to evaluate the efficacy of these therapies and the best sequence of optimization in this scenario.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This systematic review and network meta-analysis were performed and reported following the Cochrane Collaboration Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis statement guidelines. Our study received the appropriate ethical oversight and approval from the relevant ethical review boards.9,10

sec.title: Data source and search strategy
sec.p: We systematically searched the PUBMED (MEDLINE) and EMBASE databases, looking for RCTs from January 2013 to December 2022. Two authors (I.G.C.V.L and J.T.N.) performed a systematic review, and disagreements were resolved in a panel discussion with the senior author (E.A.B.). Study selection involved screening titles and abstracts followed by a full-text evaluation of potentially eligible studies (Supplemental Methods, Supplemental Figure 1).

The search used medical subject headings, accessible text terms, and Boolean logical operators. The complete search strategies are provided in the appendix. Study selection involved screening titles and abstracts followed by a full-text evaluation of potentially eligible studies. All records from the initial search were imported simultaneously into the Zotero reference manager. During this procedure, a third author resolved discrepancies through discussion or mediation.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: We considered studies eligible if they included: 1) patients ≥18 years old with established HFrEF; 2) admitted to the hospital for HF (HF hospitalization [HHF]) or within 6 months after an HHF; 3) RCTs comparing HF medication to a placebo/control group; 4) at least 1 month of follow-up; 5) RCTs published between January 2013 and December 2022; 6) the intervention therapy was initiated during hospitalization or in the vulnerable phase; 7) RCTs that reported on cardiovascular outcomes of interest; and 8) English language RCTs only.

sec.title: Endpoint
sec.p: The primary efficacy cardiovascular outcome was rehospitalization for HF, and the secondary endpoint was cardiovascular mortality.

sec.title: Risk of bias and quality assessment
sec.p: RCT quality assessment was conducted using Cochrane’s Risk of Bias 2 tool for randomized studies.11

sec.title: Subgroup analysis
sec.p: We performed prespecified subgroup analyses to assess the impact of different intervention therapy initiation times on the efficacy endpoints.

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: We performed prespecified sensitivity analyses with only phase 3 trials, looking to calculate the number needed to treat (NNT) to assess the impact of days alive with novel therapies and absolute risk reduction.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: We constructed a network meta-analysis model using a frequentist framework. The meta-analysis was performed using a random effects model (Mantel–Haenszel) to pool effect sizes because we anticipated considerable between-study heterogeneity. Treatments were ranked using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) score, also known as the P-score. The P-score is measured on a scale from 0 (worst) to 1 (best), with a higher score indicating the better overall performance of the competing treatment.12 To perform a network meta-analysis, we need a connected network to make comparisons between different treatment combinations.

Reporting bias was formally tested using the Egger test, which assesses the symmetry of funnel plots.13 When this was found to be nonsignificant, we considered the risk of reporting bias as “low.” Indirectness, which captures transitivity in the network, was assessed as low based on published guidelines. Transitivity means that we can learn about the relative treatment effect of treatment A versus treatment B from an indirect comparison via treatment C.14 Imprecision compares the treatment effects included in the 95% CI with the range of equivalence using clinically important effects as OR of 2.0. All analyses among study heterogeneity of risk estimates were examined using a standard chi-square test and I2 statistic for heterogeneity with the DerSimonian-Laird estimator. I2 is the percentage of variance that is due to between-study variance. Results are presented as ORs with 95% CIs and P values. Also, for phase 3 trials, the estimated effect on the outcome was expressed as a relative risk (RR) with a 95% CI, compared to the placebo-control. The NNT was calculated based on the absolute risk reduction derived from the meta-analytic estimates. The NNT represents the average number of patients who need to be treated with the intervention instead of the placebo for 1 additional patient to benefit. All reported probability values are 2-tailed, and a P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. The random effects network meta-analysis was performed using the “netmeta package” in R (R Foundation, version 4.2.2).15

sec.title: Results
sec.p:
Searching the different databases yielded a total of 2,311 potential articles. After screening the abstracts and removing duplicates, 18 studies were retrieved for full-text analysis. We performed a full-text analysis of the studies, and 9 trials were selected according to our strict selection criteria (Table 1). We had 3 direct comparison studies using SGLT2 inhibitors (2 with empagliflozin and 1 with sotagliflozin) and other 5 direct comparison studies investigating ARNI, ferric carboxymaltose, vericiguat, omecamtiv-mecarbil, and finerenone. Most studies reported that the medication was initiated during hospitalization. We had 2 phase-II trials assessing vericiguat and finerenone, with a secondary efficacy endpoint. sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p:
HHF was reported in all studies, which enrolled a total of 18,540 patients. The largest reductions in HHF were seen with sotagliflozin (OR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.39-0.63; P < 0.0001), followed by ARNI (OR: 0.54; 95% CI: 0.35-0.83; P = 0.005), ferric carboxymaltose (OR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.44-0.70; P < 0.0001), empagliflozin (OR: 0.56; 95% CI: 0.39-0.78; P = 0.0007), vericiguat 10 mg (OR: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.74-0.92; P = 0.0008), and finerenone 15 mg (OR: 0.59; 95% CI: 0.38-0.91; P = 0.016). Omecamtiv-mecarbil (OR: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.81-1.01, P = 0.0682) and other doses of vericiguat and finerenone did not reduce the risk of the primary outcome (Figure 1A). Quantified heterogeneity/inconsistency was 0% (tau2 = 0; tau = 0; I2 = 0%, 0% to 89.6%).Figure 1
Forest Plot for Heart Failure Hospitalization and Cardiovascular Mortality Against Control
Data are reported as ORs compared to placebo/control, which is the reference group. The P-score is measured on a scale from 0 (worst) to 1 (best), with a higher score indicating the better overall performance of the competing treatment. (A) Represents the effect of interventions on hospitalization for heart failure, showing odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) compared to control. (B) Represents the effect of interventions on cardiovascular mortality, showing odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) compared to control. Abbreviation as in Figure 1.

Only the finerenone trial (ARTS-HF) did not report cardiovascular mortality. The largest reduction in cardiovascular death was seen with empagliflozin (OR: 0.48; 95% CI: 0.23-0.97; P = 0.04). Vericiguat 10 mg (OR: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.74-1.10; P = 0.33), ferric carboxymaltose (OR: 0.97; 95% CI: 0.69-1.36; P = 0.31), ARNI (OR: 0.66; 95% CI: 0.29-1.49; P = 0.33), omecamtiv-mecarbil (OR: 0.92; 95%-CI: 0.79-1.08; P = 0.32), sotagliflozin (OR: 0.88; 95% CI: 0.58-1.30; P = 0.51), and other doses of vericiguat did not reduce the risk of the secondary outcome (Figure 1B). Quantified heterogeneity/inconsistency was 0% (tau2 = 0; tau = 0; I2 = 0%, 0% to 89.6%).

sec.title: Treatment ranking
sec.p:
In our graphical representation of rank scores, the compounds exhibiting the highest likelihood of achieving a significant reduction in the risk of HF readmission were as follows: sotagliflozin (P-score 0.88), followed by ARNI (P-score 0.81), ferric carboxymaltose (P-score 0.80), empagliflozin (P-score 0.78), finerenone 15 mg (P-score 0.76), vericiguat 5 mg (P-score 0.67), and finerenone 10 mg (P-score 0.61). In contrast, vericiguat 2.5 mg (P-score 0.17), vericiguat 1.25 mg (P-score 0.17), and finerenone 5 mg (P-score 0.16) displayed the lowest likelihood of efficacy (Central Illustration, Figure 2, and Supplemental Figure 2).Figure 2
Network Plots and League Tables of Heart Failure Hospitalization and Cardiovascular Mortality
Network plots and league tables of (A) heart failure hospitalization and (B) cardiovascular mortality endpoints comparing novel heart failure therapies. Network plots: The nodes represent the novel heart failure therapies to be compared, and the edges represent the observed direct comparisons in the included trials. The size of nodes is proportional to the number of patients assigned to the treatment regimen, and the thickness of the edges is proportional to the sample size of each study. sec.title: Evaluation of inconsistency
sec.p: The majority of comparisons did not show concerns for imprecision. Comparisons that showed major concerns for imprecision largely involved 2 single phase II studies investigating vericiguat (SOCRATES-Reduced [Soluble Guanylate Cyclase Stimulator in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction Study]) and finerenone (ARTS-HF [Mineralocorticoid Receptor antagonist Tolerability Study-Heart Failure]) but with no statistical significance (total [Q = 1.79, d.f. = 2, P = 0.40], within designs [Q = 0.69, d.f. = 1, P = 0.40], and between designs [Q = 1.10, d.f = 1, P = 0.29]) (Supplemental Figure 3).

sec.title: Subgroup and sensitivity analysis
sec.p: Subgroup analyses were performed restricting to the time period of medication initiation for hospitalization for HF and cardiovascular mortality endpoints. Overall, results remained similar to the primary analysis, but there was a trend of reducing primary and secondary endpoints when medications were initiated predischarge. Subgroup analysis results are presented in Supplemental Figures 4 and 5.

The RR of the interventions ranged from 0.24 for (intervention with the lowest RR, with empagliflozin) to 0.92 for (intervention with the highest RR, with omecamtiv-mercabil), with corresponding NNT extending from 3.86 to 51.05, indicating a broad spectrum of clinical effectiveness. Notably, the EMPULSE (Empagliflozin in Patients Hospitalized With Acute Heart Failure) trial showed an RR of 0.77 with an NNT of 3.86, suggesting that treating approximately 4 patients could prevent 1 additional adverse outcome compared to placebo. Similarly, the SOLOIST-WHF trial, with sotagliflozin, reported an RR of 0.66 and an NNT of 4.14, underscoring the potential benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors. Conversely, the GALACTIC-HF trial exhibited a more modest effect with an RR of 0.92 and the highest NNT of 51.05, indicating that over 50 patients would require treatment to avert 1 adverse event compared to placebo (Supplemental Figure 6).

The pooled analyses across key HF therapies, including ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers, MRAs, left ventricular ejection fraction, and New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classes II and III, consistently demonstrated statistically significant benefits with no evidence of heterogeneity in any subgroup (I2 = 0%, P > 0.99). ACEI/ARB therapy showed a pooled effect size of 4.28 (95% CI: 1.48-7.08), and beta-blockers similarly yielded a significant effect of 4.40 (95% CI: 1.53-7.28), indicating robust improvements across studies despite some uncertainty in individual study results. MRA therapy had a pooled effect size of 3.56 (95% CI: 1.18-5.94), and left ventricle ejection fraction analysis showed an improvement of 3.40 (95% CI: 1.18-5.63), both confirming statistically significant benefits. For NYHA functional class II, the pooled effect was 3.36 (95% CI: 1.12-5.59), and for NYHA functional class III, it was 3.91 (95% CI: 1.35-6.47), further emphasizing the positive impact of these interventions on functional status and clinical outcomes. Across all subgroups, the absence of heterogeneity indicates that the benefits of these therapies are consistent and generalizable across different patient populations. Although, the ARTS trial (with finerenone), frequently had a nonsignificant effect size, may suggest that this medication was affected by baseline HF therapy and clinical conditions (Supplemental Figures 7 to 12).

sec.title: Risk of bias and publication bias
sec.p: The Cochrane Collaboration tool was used for quality assessment. All studies had a low overall bias. There was no evidence of systematic reporting bias for the primary endpoint (Egger test P = 0.06) (Supplemental Figure 13 and 16).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our network meta-analysis sheds light on managing WHF in patients with reduced ejection fraction. The main results of this network meta-analysis are as follows. 1) The introduction of SGLT2 inhibitors during hospitalization and, subsequently, integration of ARNI and iron infusion significantly reduce HF readmission. 2) Notably, empagliflozin emerges as a pivotal agent with a slight reduction in cardiovascular mortality with a low NNT. 3) In our subgroup analysis, the introduction during hospitalization led to a higher risk reduction of events. The marked reduction in HF readmissions underscored by our findings provides valuable insights into a high-risk patient population often underrepresented in the existing literature.

Current guidelines do not clearly recommend how to optimize the GDMT for HFrEF during a HHF. The studies included in this network meta-analysis enrolled predischarge hospitalized patients or recent postdischarge patients, providing valuable insights into managing the GDMT in this vulnerable phase. Our results support the current practice of introducing GDMT as quickly as possible and suggest that we should expand GDMT to prevent rehospitalization in patients with WHF who are at high residual risk. For patients taking an ACEI or ARB and whose condition worsens despite background therapy, our findings support the use of switching to an ARNI during hospitalization. However, this finding is based on a single study.15

The most clinically meaningful benefit and the best choice as first-line therapy in our analysis were SGLT2 inhibitors (sotagliflozin and empagliflozin). Even though a small sample size might limit studies evaluating these medications, our study suggests that SGLT2i must be part of “quadruple” therapy for a high residual risk of readmission. Also, empagliflozin, when initiated predischarge, was the only drug capable of leading to a slight reduction in the secondary outcome of cardiovascular mortality. The ongoing RCTs NCT04363697, NCT05406505, and NCT03200860 will provide additional information in this regard. In SOLOIST5 and EMPULSE16 trials included in this analysis, about 17% of the patients were medicated with ARNI, 80% with beta-blockers, and 70% with ACEI or ARB; this low rate of background therapy prescription may have influenced the magnitude of the effect found. This divergence may result from differences in trial populations, follow-up durations, and risk profiles influencing outcomes. Additionally, competitive risk theory provides insight into why mortality benefits might appear muted: patients with HF often experience competing risks from comorbidities or other high-risk conditions, potentially diminishing the apparent impact of interventions on mortality endpoints. Furthermore, many trials may lack sufficient power to detect significant differences in secondary endpoints like cardiovascular mortality, especially when the primary endpoint focuses on short-term rehospitalization. Omecamtiv-mecarbil and vericiguat reduced rehospitalizations without impacting mortality. This may reflect both the targeted short-term efficacy of these agents and the limitations inherent in the trials’ designs and statistical power. Recognizing these factors is essential for interpreting the clinical implications of our findings, as they suggest that some therapies may offer immediate benefits in reducing hospitalization without necessarily extending long-term survival.

In the VICTORIA trial8 (vericiguat 10 mg) and GALACTIC trial6 (omecamtiv-mercabil), we noticed a higher rate of prescription of background therapy (beta-blockers and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors) and a higher rate of patients with functional class III and IV. However, the rate of composite primary events of death or hospitalization due to HF in these studies was lower than in comparator studies; despite differences in population, our pairwise comparison shows that this choice of treatment may have an additional risk reduction, but the network estimate generated by indirect comparison had inconsistency.

Finerenone is a nonsteroidal MRA that has been shown to reduce the risk of hospitalization for HF and cardiovascular death in patients with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes. In the ARTS-HF trial,17 finerenone reduced the risk of hospitalization for HF by 17% in decompensated patients. Still, the information about the use of ARNI or SGLT2i in ARTS-HF trial was not available, so the incremental reduction of HF decompensation may decrease when compared with a well-medicated population. We have evaluated the efficacy and safety of steroidal MRA (spironolactone and eplerenone) prescription, but finerenone may have an additional efficacy over steroidal MRA. However, more research is needed to confirm its long-term efficacy in this patient population.

Several trials tried to evaluate the effect of intravenous iron replacement in HFrEF, but most of these included patients in a stable context and did not provide consistent information about this topic. AFFIRM-AHF17 was the only 1 that included symptomatic patients with acute HF and iron deficiency. A risk reduction in HHF comparable with the other drugs was unexpected. Still, one possible reason for these results was an event rate higher than in other trials, which may be due to the inclusion of a higher-risk population. Also, iron replacement is a safe and short-duration therapy that may decrease health costs.

sec.title: Study limitations
sec.p: Several limitations identified are important to consider when interpreting the results of our network meta-analysis. First, a small number of studies and concerns about bias: Our analysis included 9 trials, a relatively small number of studies, some of which were small, which means that the results should be interpreted with caution. A key limitation of our analysis is the applicability of the findings to a broader HF population, as the included trials primarily enrolled patients with reduced ejection fraction. This focus limits the generalizability of the results to other HF phenotypes, particularly HF with preserved ejection fraction and HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction, as well as those with complex comorbid profiles. Patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction or HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction present distinct pathophysiological characteristics and may respond differently to the therapies analyzed. To ensure that novel interventions can be effectively applied across the full spectrum of HF patients, future studies should aim to include a more diverse range of phenotypes. This would provide insights into the efficacy and safety of treatments across varying HF subtypes and support more inclusive clinical recommendations. Second, a low background therapy prescription rate in several trials is another potential limitation. This means the results may not apply to patients already receiving maximal doses of GDMT. Third, the fact that the estimates of the effects of these agents were based on single large phase III trials means that there are limited data to confirm their long-term safety and efficacy. Lastly, we must acknowledge that the trials included in our network meta-analysis had varying follow-up periods and population size concerns, which may influence the results. Ideally, HRs would be preferred for addressing time-to-event outcomes such as HHF and cardiovascular mortality. However, the majority of the RCTs included in our analysis reported ORs. Converting ORs to HRs without detailed survival data, such as Kaplan-Meier curves, would introduce significant uncertainty and potentially compromise the robustness of the results. To maintain methodological consistency and ensure accurate comparisons between studies, we opted to use ORs across the analysis. We encourage future studies to report HRs for time-dependent outcomes like cardiovascular mortality.

Additionally, while ORs are known to potentially overestimate effect sizes in studies with longer follow-up periods, key trials such as SOLOIST and AFFIRM-AHF demonstrated significant treatment benefits within the first 3 months of follow-up. This supports the validity of our findings, despite the limitations of not having HRs reported in all studies. We also acknowledge that variability in follow-up durations and population sizes may influence event rates and the robustness of our conclusions.

Long-term data are insufficient to properly assess rehospitalization, mortality, and quality of life. Many of the included trials either lack extended follow-up or have not yet published their long-term results. This absence of data limits our ability to fully evaluate the durability and sustained effectiveness of the therapies in these key endpoints. Future analyses should incorporate extended follow-up results as they become available to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the outcomes. Nonetheless, the consistency observed across heterogeneity analyses and the benefits identified early in the follow-up period strengthen the reliability of our results. Discrepancies in safety endpoints among the RCTs pose challenges to the network's transitivity, potentially affecting the consistency of indirect treatment comparisons. Despite this, our findings remain invaluable for optimizing GDMT during the precarious phase of HHF, advocating for the proactive integration of SGLT2 inhibitors, ferric carboxymaltose, and ARNI into treatment protocols. Overall, our network meta-analysis provides valuable insights into the potential benefits of novel therapies for reducing the risk of HF readmission in hospitalized patients, and these are the best available data to this moment.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p:
This network meta-analysis comparing novel therapy regiments for patients with WHF, beginning with SGLT2 inhibitors during hospitalization and subsequently integrating ARNI and iron infusion, could optimize outcomes. In addition, empagliflozin emerges as a pivotal agent with a slight reduction in cardiovascular mortality. Our subgroup analysis indicates that initiating these treatments during hospitalization may be preferable to waiting until the vulnerable phase postdischarge. These insights offer a foundation for treatment strategies during the acute phase of HF, filling a gap left by the absence of head-to-head trials and potentially influencing future guidelines.Perspectives
COMPETENCY IN SYSTEMS-BASED MEDICINE: Our systematic review and network meta-analysis suggest that starting novel treatments like SGLT2 inhibitors, ARNI, and ferric carboxymaltose during hospitalization significantly lowers rehospitalization risk for WHF, enhancing guideline-directed therapy and reducing future admissions.
TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: Adequately powered randomized trials are needed to compare the novel therapies in WHF scenarios.
